transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Dev (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood SE), Daniel (Mariner Head of ML), Priya (Mariner Platform), Samir (Mariner Ops)

Summary (auto): quick Optimize console walkthrough focused on sessionization, prefetch (prefix/KV) strategy and an initial costing model. Agreement to run a 2-week Dedicated pilot and share sample traffic for realistic bench.

00:00 Sofia: okay everyone uh thanks for joining, I'm Sofia from Redwood, I'll do quick context then Dev will walk through the console and cost sim.
00:07 Daniel: yep thanks, we've been evaluating a few inference runtimes, want to see how batching + prefetch actually impacts unit cost for our customer chat flows.
00:12 Dev: cool, that's the goal — we'll show the Optimize console, the savings sim, and then a sandbox plan. Quick qual question — what are your latency SLOs for user-facing chat?
00:21 Priya: p95 under 350ms ideally, tail matters a lot. We're comfortable with up to 500ms if it means big cost wins. Also we run a mix of short prompts (one-shots) and long conversation sessions with history.
00:34 Dev: got it. And roughly what's your concurrency at peak, and sessionization behavior?
00:40 Samir: peak concurrency about 1.2k rps, but sessions are sticky — about 60% of traffic are returning sessions with history length distribution skewed to 50-200 tokens. New sessions are ~40% and usually shorter.
00:53 Dev: perfect, that's very similar to other insurance workflows we see. Ok jumping into the console — apologies if the auto-transcribe shows 'Redwood counsel' sometimes — the Optimize tab has a cost simulator, batching slider, prefetch (KV/prefix) toggle, and an estimated hit-rate model.
01:05 Maya: note, the prefetch option supports both prefix-only caching (we cache the left context prefixes) and full KV session cache where we store the key-value attention cache for active sessions. Prefetch tends to give big wins for warm sessions, KV cache gives greatest latency reduction for long-history sessions.
01:20 Dev: showing a baseline: no-batching, no-prefetch, default hosted model (gpt-ish open model) cost about $X per million tokens — [transcription glitch, number fuzzy] — but in our spreadsheet we converted to per-request cost for Mariner's distribution.
01:35 Daniel: can you walk through a concrete example? numbers help.
01:38 Dev: sure. Assume: average request tokens = 120 input + 40 output = 160 total tokens. Baseline throughput with no batching: average latency 220ms, cost per req = 160 tokens * unit_cost. For simplicity in the sim we set unit token cost of $0.000012 per token, so per-request token cost ~ $0.00192. For 10M requests that's about $19.2k.
02:06 Dev: now add batching: if we can get an effective batch size of 8 at similar latency, compute amortization on model decode cost — that reduces per-request cost roughly by (1 - 1/8) on the decoder compute portion. In their workload, with short outputs the effective token parallelism saves ~25-30% in serving cost.
02:28 Priya: how did you pick batch=8? our peak concurrency and arrival curve might allow higher.
02:33 Dev: good question — the sim uses arrival curve and tail latency to solve for batching that keeps p95 under target. For Mariner we tuned for p95 under 350ms; with your concurrency the simulator predicts safe batch sizes 6-10 in hosted, maybe up to 16 in Dedicated with more headroom.
02:50 Maya: and then prefetch/KV: prefix prefetch gives hit-rates based on returned session heatmap. If 45% of sessions are warm with repeated prefixes, prefix caching can short-circuit up to 40% of decoding tokens for those requests. If you combine with batching, we typically see multiplicative savings.
03:08 Dev: putting numbers: baseline 10M reqs -> $19.2k. Add batching (batch=8) => 28% savings -> $13.8k. Add prefix prefetch with a 50% hit rate on outputs for warm sessions (which are 60% of traffic) -> additional 20% overall token reduction -> down to ~$11k. If we add KV session cache (store full KV) you get lower latency and higher hit for long histories — saves another maybe 10% and reduces p95 dramatically.
03:36 Daniel: so you're saying combined we could be near 40-50% cost reduction?
03:39 Dev: yes, in many cases 35-55% relative to naive baseline depending on hit rates and batch efficiency. Important caveat: prefetch and KV rely on session stickiness and TTLs — if sessions are ephemeral it's less effective.
03:52 Priya: we have session TTLs of 48h but we prune inactive sessions after 12h for storage. Does Redwood need longer TTL for KV?
03:59 Maya: you can configure TTLs per workload. The console shows tradeoffs — longer TTL increases storage but raises hit rates. We have integrated KMS for encryption of cached blobs (mentions of K M S in the transcribe may be spelled KMS or 'kay-ems').
04:14 Dev: switching to the savings sim view — here's the heatmap you sent, Priya, (we anonymized) showing session concentration: 20% of sessions account for 65% of repeated prefixes — that suggests prefetch will be very effective.
04:26 Priya: that's good to see. On the legal side, do you log cached content? we need SOC 2 and auditable eviction logs.
04:33 Sofia: yes — SOC 2 in our packet, we keep audit logs for cache operations, and you can disable storing LLM outputs in cache if needed. For private/Dedicated deployments we support customer-managed KMS and VPC peering so data residency is preserved.
04:47 Samir: what's the operational complexity? sounds like a lot of knobs.
04:50 Dev: it can be, but Optimize includes recommended configurations per workload: a suggested batch size, prefetch threshold, and TTL. The recommendation engine uses your traffic distribution, model seq lengths, and latency SLO to pick a Pareto point. You can also run the 'savings sandbox' which simulates 2 weeks of traffic against different configs and outputs projected spend and p95.
05:08 Dev: quick demo — toggling from hosted to Dedicated changes the sim assumptions: Dedicated gives higher safe batching (so more savings) but you trade committing to reserved capacity. The simulator shows cost per effective request including committed cost amortized across expected traffic.
05:22 Daniel: any guidance on running a pilot? we want realistic numbers.
05:26 Sofia: typical flow — 1) share sample traffic CSV (timestamps, session id, token counts), 2) Redwood runs a sandbox sim and shares cost scenarios, 3) we provision a small Dedicated pool or full-privately-hosted test and run a 2-week bench with real requests, 4) review results and tune prefetch thresholds before rollout.
05:43 Dev: for the bench we'll use both synthetic warmup and your real traffic to capture prefix hit behavior. We'll instrument the trace IDs and return a detailed per-route cost and latency breakdown in the console.
05:52 Priya: latency of prefetch itself — does prefetch add latency for cold sessions?
05:55 Maya: minimal. Prefix prefetch warms up likely continuations asynchronously and only blocks when a cold miss happens. KV cache on the hot path reduces decode work so it reduces latency for warm sessions significantly. There's sometimes a small head-of-line blocking if prefetch triggers network IO, but we hide that with background warmers and local memory caches on the node.
06:15 Daniel: competitor question — some vendors promise simpler configs but less observability. Do you have per-token attribution to see exactly where saving occurs?
06:23 Dev: yes — per-request token breakdown (prompt vs generation vs KV hit savings), trace ids, and cost attribution are available in the Console under 'Route cost breakdown'. You can export to CSV for your FinOps team.
06:33 Samir: any hard limits on KV size per session?
06:36 Maya: default per-session KV cap is configurable; we recommend capping at the 95th percentile token history to control storage. The Optimize sim runs scenarios for different caps and shows marginal benefits.
06:48 Dev: quick objection handling — if you're worried about quality regressions from quantization or batching, Redwood Optimize ties back into the evals plane: we run prompt sets to ensure quality delta under 2% for metrics you care about.
06:59 Daniel: okay that helps. One more thing — organization-wise, who would own the pilot on your side?
07:04 Priya: Platform team (me) will own infra, ML will validate quality (Daniel), Ops (Samir) will monitor rollout.
07:10 Sofia: great. Recap and next steps: we'll send cost spreadsheet and a baseline sim exported from today's demo; Dev will prepare bench scripts and test plan; Mariner will provide traffic CSV and confirm pilot start window.
07:22 Daniel: sounds good. Anything else?
07:25 Dev: I'll also add a note about fallback policies — auto-fallback to smaller model if smart routing sees capacity issues; helps reliability.
07:33 Priya: please include the SOC 2 + KMS integration docs in the packet.
07:36 Sofia: will do. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with meeting notes and the files.

Auto notes: Speakers overlapped occasionally; some transcription artifacts ('Redwood counsel', 'kay em ess', numbers fuzzy).

End.
